To summarize, the key findings of our research, stated in one sentence that includes all relevant information, are that

animal viruses, some of them possibly unable to replicate in humans, could be transmitted from animals to people where they might be linked to tumour diseases currently not attributed to viral infections.

the following viruses may cause cancer in humans: (i) human papillomaviruses (HPV), (ii) hepatitis B and hepatitis C viruses, (iii) Epstein-Barr virus (EBV) and (iv) human T cell leukaemia/lymphoma virus (HTLV).
animal viruses, some of them unable to replicate in humans, could be transmitted from animals to humans, where they may be associated with human cancer.
In summary, our research is concerned with
the following questions: - What is the risk of acquiring animal viruses from animals?
the following questions: 1) What are the possible causes of human cancer?
the following questions: 1) Are there animal viruses that are unable to replicate in humans but are able to induce tumours?
In summary, a comprehensive and detailed conclusive statement would be that

animal viruses with oncogenic potential in non-human systems may be involved in some human cancers, but the extent of this involvement is unknown and the risk of transmission of such viruses to humans is probably small.

animal viruses, some of them possibly not able to replicate in human cell systems, could be transmitted from animals to humans where they may be associated with tumours currently not linked to viruses.
the possibility that human tumours may have a viral aetiology is not ruled out.
A comprehensive summary for our work would be that
animal viruses, some of them unable to replicate in humans, may be transmitted to people and may be linked to human cancers.
animal virus oncogenesis should be studied in non-permissive hosts, and that human tumours should be examined for proliferation-inducing animal virus genomes.

animal viruses, some of them probably unable to replicate or induce tumours in human cells, may have been transmitted to humans where they may be associated with human tumours currently not attributable to viruses.
The main takeaway from our work is that
there are many animal viruses that are oncogenic in animals but not in humans and that there may be human cancers that are not yet recognized as virus-associated.
there may be many more viruses than we thought that can cause cancer.
we should not ignore the possibility of viruses that have not been previously linked to human cancers as a cause for some of them.
